increments.title: Every address form in DR1 labels the same two fields "Postcode or Zip code" and "Phone number"; the frontend labels them "Postal or zip code" and "Telephone number".
increments.detail:
Wherever the frontend asks a user to type an address rather than pick one, the postcode field is labelled "Postal or zip code" and the phone field "Telephone number". The private transporter form shows both, and its captured page renders them exactly so (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/transport/private-transporter-details/private-transporter-details.njk:58-59,74-75, strings at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/transport/copy/copy.en.js:108,110). The permanent-address block inside the animal identification card repeats the same two labels from its own copy file (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/commodities/copy/copy.en.js:102,105), and so do the validation messages on both forms. So the two strings are authored twice, in two feature copy files, and both spellings disagree with DR1.

DR1 authors both labels once per form partial and spells them the same way every time: "Postcode or Zip code" and "Phone number". The private transporter form uses them (app/views/partials/transporter-add-private-fields.html:62,100), and so do the address book's manual add form and the permanent-address new-address form, which are the other two places DR1 asks a user to type an address. The captured private transporter page renders both.

Change both labels to DR1's wording in each feature copy file that holds them — the transport copy and the commodities copy — and bring the matching validation messages with them, since each names the field it is about. Two strings in two files, and no behaviour changes. Do it in one pass rather than per form, because the point of the change is that every address form in the service asks for the same thing in the same words.

increments.title: DR1 calls the sending party "Consignor"; the frontend calls it "Consignor or exporter" on the hub and as the picker's heading.
increments.detail:
One copy entry, `consignor: { title: 'Consignor or exporter' }` (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/copy/copy.en.js:20-21), supplies both the hub row title (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/controller.js:33-35,49) and the picker's h1 (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/party-picker/party-picker.njk:8). fe-addresses-hub renders it as "Consignor or exporter" wrapping onto two lines in the summary-list key.

DR1 names the same party "Consignor" everywhere a user sees it — the hub section heading, the picker h1 and the add link "Add a consignor" (app/data/consignment-address-sections.js:17-19, rendered at app/views/roles-and-addresses.html:49 and app/views/consignment-address-select.html:42). Only the internal section id keeps the longer form, `consignor-or-exporter`. Both sides give the same hint under it, "This is the sender of the consignment."

Change the user-facing label to "Consignor" in the addresses copy, which carries it to the hub row, the picker heading and the breadcrumb. This is a term change rather than a rewording: "or exporter" names a second legal role that DR1 does not put in front of the trader, and both sides describe the party identically in the hint, so nothing about who to enter changes. The route slug and the stored answer key stay as they are, matching DR1, which also kept the longer form internally. The validation message "Select a consignor from the list" (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/copy/copy.en.js:23) already uses the shorter term, so the page contradicts itself today.

increments.title: DR1 tells the trader what a consignment contact address is; the frontend only tells them what happens when they pick one.
increments.detail:
The only guidance on the page is the radios' hint, "Selecting a contact copies their name and address into this notification." (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/contact/copy/copy.en.js:4, rendered at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/contact/template.njk:20). It describes what the control does, which the trader can see for themselves, and says nothing about who the contact should be or what they are being signed up for. fe-contact then lists thirteen organisations with no basis on which to choose between them.

DR1 opens the page with a definition of the role: "This is the contact address of the person responsible for the consignment from when it enters Great Britain until authorities complete their checks." (app/views/contact-address-for-consignment.html:50-52). The list beneath it is headed "Select an address" (:62), so the definition sits between the h1 and the choice, where a trader reads it before deciding.

Replace the mechanism sentence with DR1's definition, as an intro paragraph between the heading and the radios rather than as a hint on the fieldset. The sentence carries a real obligation — it tells the trader the contact must be reachable through border checks — which is the thing the frontend currently leaves them to guess.

increments.title: DR1 offers only the trader's own GB branch addresses as the consignment contact; the frontend offers the whole address book, overseas consignors included.
increments.detail:
The contact page offers `addressBook.all(orgId)` — every record in the organisation's book, in book order (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/contact/controller.js:69-74). fe-contact shows thirteen radios, the same thirteen records the party pickers page through, and they include Astra Rosales in Switzerland, Danish Meat Export ApS in Denmark, Laiterie du Nord SARL in France and Iberian Swine SA in Spain. So a trader can name a Spanish exporter as the person responsible for the consignment once it is inside Great Britain, and nothing on the page discourages it. The address book holds no type by which the list could be narrowed — the service says so in its own contract, "Addresses have no type in the address book (D3) — the same record may be a consignor on one notification and a consignee on the next" (src/server/app/services/address-book/index.js:12-15).

DR1 draws this list from a separate collection of branch addresses, not from the consignment address book the pickers use (app/data/contact-addresses.js:1-21, rendered at app/views/contact-address-for-consignment.html:68-83). dr1-contact-address-for-consignment shows three, all in Great Britain: Aberdeen Livestock Ltd in Aberdeen, West Country Livestock Ltd in Bristol, Cymru Animal Imports Ltd in Cardiff. The page says what the list is for — the person responsible for the consignment from when it enters Great Britain — and the help line names the collection when it tells the trader where a missing one comes from: "add a new branch address" (:65).

Narrow the contact list to the trader's own branch addresses. That needs the address book to distinguish a branch record from a party record, which today it deliberately does not, so the API and the record shape have to change before the page can. Until then the page offers a choice DR1 rules out, and the frontend's own hint does not warn against it. The narrower question of what the page says the contact is for is a separate copy change on the same page.

FALSIFIED BY: A DR1 contact list drawn from the same address collection as the consignment pickers, or an address-book record carrying a type or category the frontend could filter on today.

The frontend page renders thirteen radios, and the four overseas records the finding names are all there — Astra Rosales in Bern, Danish Meat Export ApS in Copenhagen, Laiterie du Nord SARL in Lille and Iberian Swine SA in Huesca. increments.title: DR1 asks for a CPH number on every consignment except horses and the 01061900 group; the frontend asks only when the consignment contains cattle.
increments.detail:
The CPH row appears on the addresses hub, and the CPH page is reachable, only when a commodity line matches a whitelist of one entry: `CPH_COMMODITIES = ['Cow']` (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/services/commodities/stub.js:119, applied by src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/cph-number/controller.js:27-30 and src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/controller.js:50-52). Everything else in the catalogue — horses, cats, dogs and fish — is never asked for a CPH number. The rule is an allow-list, so every commodity added to the catalogue from now on defaults to not being asked.

DR1 works the opposite way round: the CPH section is in the default set of address sections, and a commodity code has to be listed explicitly to escape it (app/data/consignment-address-sections.js:148-160). Two live-animal codes escape — 0101, horses, and 01061900, the cat/dog/ferret group, which gets a permanent-address section instead (:101,124). Cattle and pigs are listed explicitly with CPH included (:108,116), and every other live-animal code in DR1's catalogue, from sheep and goats through poultry to ornamental fish, falls to the default and is asked for one. Two germinal-product codes, 05111000 and 05119985, are also listed without CPH (:132,139), but germinal products are outside this comparison, so they neither add to nor subtract from the rule for live animals.

Invert the rule: ask for a CPH number unless the consignment's commodity is one that is exempt, and make the exempt list horses and the 01061900 group rather than making cattle the only inclusion. Within today's five-entry catalogue this changes one commodity, fish, which DR1 asks and the frontend does not; the reason to do it anyway is that the allow-list makes every future commodity silently exempt, which is the wrong default for a question DR1 treats as the norm. Whether each newly-included commodity really needs a CPH number is a question for the catalogue work rather than for this rule.

FALSIFIED BY: A live-animal commodity code in DR1's catalogue, outside 0101 and 01061900, that is not asked for a CPH number, which would mean the default set is incidental rather than the rule.

finding.correction: Claim corrected, finding stands. It said only two commodity codes escape the CPH default. Four do: 0101 and 01061900 as claimed, and also 05111000 and 05119985. Checked by reading the whole code-to-sections map rather than the two entries the finding named. The two extra codes are germinal products — semen, embryos and ova — which the finding contract puts outside this comparison, so the rule the finding describes holds for every live-animal code in DR1's catalogue: 0102 and 0103 name CPH explicitly, and 010410, 010420, the 01051x poultry range, 010613, 010614, 010620, 010632, 010633, 01064100 and 030111 all fall to the default and get it. The prototype slot and the falsifier are amended to say live-animal, because as originally written the falsifier fired on the finding's own evidence. The frontend half needed no change: the allow-list really is one entry, `CPH_COMMODITIES = ['Cow']`, and the frontend's fish carries code 0301, which under DR1's rule falls to the default and is asked — so the one-commodity blast radius inside today's catalogue is right. The medium confidence is right too: with five commodities in the catalogue the rule itself cannot be watched working, only read. One caution about how it is argued: "invert the allow-list" is a statement about the shape of the rule rather than about what a user meets, and a finding whose substance is a code difference is not a finding. This one survives because it has a user-facing core underneath — a trader importing ornamental fish is asked for a CPH number in DR1 and is not asked in the frontend — and that is the sentence to lead with when the work is picked up.
finding.falsifiedBy: A live-animal commodity code in DR1's catalogue, outside 0101 and 01061900, that is not asked for a CPH number, which would mean the default set is incidental rather than the rule.

relatedTo.why: how much the rule change matters depends on how far the catalogue grows past its five entries

increments.title: DR1's CPH page explains what a CPH number is and where to find one, behind a "What is a CPH number?" expander; the frontend page carries no help content at all.
increments.detail:
The page opens on the error summary and goes straight to the form and the single input (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/cph-number/template.njk:6-25); the copy file holds a title, a label, a hint and three error messages, and no help strings (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/cph-number/copy/copy.en.js:1-12). fe-cph-number is a heading, an example and a box. A trader who does not know what a CPH number is, or does not know they have one, has nothing on the page to work from and no route to finding out.

Between the heading and the input DR1 puts a govukDetails summarised "What is a CPH number?" holding two paragraphs: "A county parish holding (CPH) number is a unique 9-digit number used to identify land and buildings where livestock are kept, moved or handled." and "You can find your CPH number on documents from the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA) or by checking your holding details on GOV.UK.", with the last clause a link (app/views/cph-number.html:45-51). dr1-cph-number shows it collapsed, above the field, so it costs a trader who already knows nothing.

Add the expander with both paragraphs, above the input. The GOV.UK destination for the second paragraph is still open — DR1's own href is a placeholder — so either the real holding-details page has to be found or the second paragraph ships without the link, naming APHA documents only.

FALSIFIED BY: Any help content about what a CPH number is appearing on the frontend page or in its copy file.

increments.title: The frontend's CPH example teaches a 3/3/3 grouping that no CPH number uses; DR1's example is 12/345/6789.
increments.detail:
The hint under the single input reads "For example, 123456789 or 123/456/789." (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/cph-number/copy/copy.en.js:5), and fe-cph-number renders it directly above the box. A county parish holding number is two digits of county, three of parish and four of holding, so the second example teaches a grouping that does not exist. The mistake never surfaces in testing because the controller strips the slashes before counting digits (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/cph-number/controller.js:77), so a trader who copies the pattern still passes validation — the only casualty is the trader who now believes their number is wrongly formatted, or who transcribes it into the wrong grouping elsewhere.

DR1 hints the same question with "For example 12/345/6789" (app/views/partials/cph-number-input.html:14), placed above all three boxes so it explains the whole number rather than any one part. The 2/3/4 shape it teaches is the shape the three boxes enforce through their widths and maxlengths (:21,33,45).

Change the example to the real grouping, "For example 12/345/6789". Keep the unslashed alternative only if content design wants it, and if so make it consistent with the grouping. Nothing about validation changes: the controller already accepts both forms.

FALSIFIED BY: APHA publishing CPH numbers in a 3/3/3 grouping, which would make the frontend's example right and DR1's wrong.

increments.title: DR1 collects the CPH number as three boxes sized to its county, parish and holding parts; the frontend takes the whole number in one free-text field.
increments.detail:
One govukInput at width-10 takes the whole number (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/cph-number/template.njk:11-23). fe-cph-number shows a single empty box with nothing to say how the nine digits divide up. On submit the controller strips slashes and checks for exactly nine digits (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/cph-number/controller.js:75-80,32-40), so "123456789", "12/345/6789" and "1/2/3456789" are all accepted and stored identically; a trader who mistypes a digit in the wrong part gets no signal, because nothing on the page knows which part is which.

DR1 uses a three-part input under the legend "CPH number" — County at width-2 and maxlength 2, Parish at width-3 and maxlength 3, Holding number at width-4 and maxlength 4, each numeric (app/views/partials/cph-number-input.html:17-53). dr1-cph-number shows the three boxes stepping up in width, which teaches the 2/3/4 shape without a word of copy. The parts post separately and are joined with slashes into "12/345/6789" when stored; the answered hub shows that slashed form (dr1-roles-and-addresses-complete).

Split the field into County, Parish and Holding number, sized 2/3/4 with numeric input modes and per-part maxlengths, and join them in the controller so the stored value stays the nine bare digits the backend already receives — the wire contract does not move. Validate each part for its own length so the error names the part that is wrong. Note that DR1 itself validates nothing on this page: the 2/3/4 shape rests on the maxlength attributes, so the frontend's nine-digit check is the stricter behaviour and should be kept.

FALSIFIED BY: GDS content or accessibility guidance for this service ruling against splitting a single reference number across three boxes — the argument that applies to a National Insurance number — in which case the single field is right and only the hint is wrong.

increments.title: DR1's addresses hub shows each party's full selected address under its own heading; the frontend hub shows the party's name and nothing else.
increments.detail:
The hub is a single govukSummaryList (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/template.njk:11). Each party is one row: the key holds the party title and its hint, the value holds the selected record's name or "Not added yet", and the action is one Add/Change link (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/controller.js:32-46). The row is built from `parties[party.id]?.name` (:49), so once a party is answered the only thing on the page is an organisation name — no address lines, no country. A trader with two similarly-named records in their address book cannot tell from the hub which one is on the notification, and the hub is the page they are sent back to after every address spoke.

Each party is a `<section>` with its own h2 heading and a hint paragraph (app/views/roles-and-addresses.html:48-50). When an address is held the section carries a govuk-inset-text block holding the record name on its own line, then every address line, then a Change link (:60-68). dr1-roles-and-addresses-complete shows this for all six sections at once — "Green Valley Farm" over five Romanian address lines under Place of origin, "Northern Livestock Imports Ltd" over three lines under Consignee and Importer, and the CPH number rendered in the same inset shape (:77-83).

Replace the summary list with one section per party: h2 heading, hint paragraph, and — when the party is answered — an inset block carrying the name, every address line and the country, with a Change link beneath it. Give the CPH row the same treatment, which is what DR1 does with it. Nothing new has to be fetched: resolveParties already returns the full record for every answered party on this request (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/controller.js:60-62), and the picker already renders address lines from the same shape (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/party-picker/view-model/address-lines.js).

FALSIFIED BY: An answered frontend hub rendering any address line beneath the party name.

finding.correction: Verified, no change, with one caveat about what was watched rather than read. The DR1 side is fully observable: the answered hub renders six inset blocks, one per section, and the place-of-origin one holds "Green Valley Farm" over five Romanian lines with a Change link inside the inset, exactly as claimed, while the CPH section takes the same shape around "12/345/6789". The frontend hub in the corpus is captured unanswered — every row reads "Not added yet" — so the claim that an answered row shows a bare organisation name comes from the row builder, which puts `parties[party.id]?.name` in the value cell and offers no second line. That is unambiguous in the source, and the structural half of the claim, one summary-list row per party with the title and hint in the key, is visible in the capture. Counting the DR1 rows did not mislead: on the answered hub the Change link sits in the same `__section-action` paragraph an unanswered section's Add link uses, distinguished only by an extra class and by being nested inside the inset, and it was the six insets that were counted, not the six links.
finding.falsifiedBy: An answered frontend hub rendering any address line beneath the party name.

relatedTo.why: the copy shortcuts live in the same per-section block, in the branch that runs when no address is held

increments.title: DR1 lets a trader add a new address from every address picker and from the contact page; the frontend gives them no way to add an address anywhere in the notification journey.
increments.detail:
Every picker ends with one button, Save and continue, and the table above it lists only what the address book already holds (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/party-picker/_address-picker.njk:69-111). fe-address-picker-place-of-origin shows the search box, the five-row table, the pagination and Save and continue, with no add control between them. The contact page is the same: thirteen radios and the save actions, nothing else (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/contact/template.njk:11-24). The address-book service states the position outright — "This service reads and never writes. The notification journey selects from the organisation's book; adding, changing and removing the records in it belongs to the INS frontend" (src/server/app/services/address-book/index.js:17-19) — and both pages' tests assert `createAddressHref` is undefined. So a trader who reaches a picker and finds their consignor is not in the book has nowhere to go from this service: they cannot finish the notification without leaving it, and nothing on the page tells them where to leave it to.

Every picker carries a secondary button, "Add a new address", between the results table and Save and continue (app/views/consignment-address-select.html:161-165). It goes to the address book's add flow carrying the party it was launched from; on completion the new record is written into that party's answer — so the trader comes back with it already selected — and a success banner is rendered at the top of the picker (:30-38). The contact page states the same route in a sentence: "If the correct address is not shown, add a new branch address, then return to this page." (app/views/contact-address-for-consignment.html:64-66).

Give the trader a way out of the dead end at the point they hit it: an "Add a new address" action on each of the five pickers and on the contact page. DR1's own shape is add-then-return-preselected with a success banner, which is what to build towards, and it needs a write path this service does not currently have — the frontend's address-book client is read-only by decision, and creation belongs to the INS front-door. This workspace has since accepted the opposite of that for now: the missing signpost is a deliberate temporary measure, and traders needing a new address hop across to the address book by themselves. So the finding names a gap against DR1 that is real and currently accepted, and the work behind it starts at a signpost naming where to go and how to get back, then reaches DR1's behaviour only with the cross-app link and the return contract. What the finding does not license is treating the bare picker as a defect to fix next.

FALSIFIED BY: Any control on a frontend picker or on the contact page that leads to adding an address, or any sentence on either page naming where to add one.

finding.correction: Premise verified; one sentence about the accepted decision was inverted and is rewritten. The premise — that the frontend has no create-address page at all, so there is no return hand-off left to compare — holds. Searching the whole frontend source for every spelling of an add-address route, link or href turns up two hits and both are tests asserting absence: the picker controller test asserts `createAddressHref` is undefined for all five parties, and the contact controller test asserts both `createAddressHref` and an `addNewAddress` copy string are undefined. The address routes are two, a GET and a POST on the picker path, with no third. The rendered picker and contact pages carry no such control. DR1's side is observable rather than inferred: the picker renders "Add a new address" as a secondary button linking to /address-book/add?from=place-of-origin, and the contact page renders the sentence with "add a new branch address" linking to /address-book/add?from=contact-address. The inverted sentence was "the interim accepted in this workspace is that traders hop across manually, which makes the minimum change a signpost". The accepted decision of 19 August says the reverse — the missing signpost itself is accepted as the temporary measure, superseding the sequencing note that had the cross-app link landing first. That does not falsify the finding, which is a parity statement against DR1, but it does change what done means, so the slot now says so.

relatedTo.why: both are links out of the picker into the address book, and both are settled by the same decision about which service owns address records

increments.title: DR1 asks, on a page of its own, where each animal will permanently live and offers the place of destination as a one-click answer; the frontend buries the same question as blank address fields inside each animal's identification record.
increments.detail:
There is no permanent-address row on the addresses hub — the hub is built from five parties plus a conditional CPH row (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/controller.js:48-53) and nothing else. The question is asked instead inside the animal identification card, as a heading "Permanent address", the sentence "A permanent address is required for this animal." and a block of blank inputs — name, two address lines, town, county, postal code, country, telephone number and email address — repeated for every animal (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/commodities/animal-identification/_identification-card.njk:43-50, fields at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/commodities/animal-identification/identifier/fields.js:32-33, labels at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/commodities/copy/copy.en.js:90-104). It appears for cats and dogs only (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/services/commodities/stub.js:115). Nothing offers the place of destination the trader has already given: to say an animal lives where the consignment is going, they retype the whole address, once per animal.

Permanent address is a section on the addresses hub, the sixth and last one a cat-or-dog trader sees, standing where the CPH section stands for everyone else, with its own bullet-list hint — a permanent address is where an animal will permanently reside and can be checked by the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA) — and an "Add a permanent address" link (app/data/consignment-address-sections.js:79-96). Behind it is one page, headed "Permanent address" with the question "Where will their permanent address be?", holding a card per animal in the consignment (app/views/permanent-address-animals.html:35,64-97). dr1-permanent-address-animals shows two cards, "Canis familiaris 1" and "Canis familiaris 2", each offering two radios: "Same as the place of destination (POD)", hinted with the destination address already on the notification, or "Enter a new address", hinted "This is where they will stay after spending 48 hours at the place of destination." It is asked for the whole 01061900 group — cat, dog, ferret and other live mammals (app/data/consignment-address-sections.js:124-131). It is one page, not two: `/permanent-address` writes "no" to the same-as-destination answer and redirects straight to the select page (app/routes.js:10789-10801), and the sibling view that asks "Are all the animals going to the place of destination?" is dead code — its renderer at app/routes.js:2780 has no callers.

Move the question out of the identification card and onto its own page, reached from a permanent-address row on the addresses hub, asking it once per animal with "Same as the place of destination" as the first option and the destination address shown as its hint. Take DR1's guidance with it — the two-bullet definition on the hub row, and the 48-hour sentence under the new-address option — since the frontend states neither today. The applicability difference (DR1 also asks it for ferrets and other live mammals) cannot be reproduced until the commodity catalogue grows past its five entries, so it rides with the catalogue rather than with this page.

FALSIFIED BY: A permanent-address entry in the frontend's addresses parties list, or a "same as the place of destination" option anywhere in the identification card.

The applicability difference (DR1 also asks it for ferrets and other live mammals) cannot be reproduced until the commodity catalogue grows past its five entries, so it rides with the catalogue rather than with this page.

First half, that the previous run's two-page claim is dead: GET /permanent-address writes "no" to the same-as-destination answer, clears the three permanent-address session keys and redirects to /permanent-address/select, and the renderer for the sibling "Are all the animals going to the place of destination?" page appears exactly once in the prototype, at its own definition, with no caller anywhere. So it is one page, and no user can reach the other. Second half, that the frontend does ask the question, matters more and also holds: the identification card renders the heading "Permanent address", the sentence "A permanent address is required for this animal." and a full set of blank address inputs whenever the commodity is cat or dog, and there is no shortcut of any kind to the place of destination. That is asked in the wrong place, not never asked, and the two are different pieces of work. Two fixes. The field list omitted telephone number and email address, which the card also collects, so it now enumerates all nine. And permanent address was called a seventh section: DR1's section array holds seven entries, but a cat-or-dog trader is shown six, because that commodity code takes permanent address instead of CPH, not as well — the slot now says which. One limit on the evidence: the frontend identification screen in the corpus was shot with cattle, which are not asked the question, so the frontend half of this finding was read in the source and confirmed against the commodity applicability list rather than seen in a picture. The DR1 half is fully visible — two cards, "Canis familiaris 1" and "Canis familiaris 2", each offering "Same as the place of destination (POD)" hinted with the Leeds destination address and "Enter a new address" hinted with the 48-hour sentence, under the two-bullet definition of what a permanent address is.

increments.title: DR1's address pickers offer only the addresses held for that role; the frontend offers the whole address book to all five, so a Danish meat exporter can be chosen as the place of origin, the consignee and the importer.
increments.detail:
All five pickers search one book and take no role: place of origin, consignor or exporter, consignee, importer and place of destination each read "Showing 5 of 13 addresses" over the same thirteen records in the same order. The service says why in its own contract — "Addresses have no type in the address book (D3) — the same record may be a consignor on one notification and a consignee on the next. So every picker searches one book, and no function here takes a role" (src/server/app/services/address-book/index.js:12-15), and the search and listing functions take an organisation and a query and nothing else (:94,103). The place-of-origin picture shows the result: the first row a trader is offered as the farm the animals set out from is Astra Rosales in Bern, followed by Tech Imports Ltd in London. Nothing on the page narrows the list and nothing warns that a record is the wrong kind of thing for the role, so the trader does the sorting themselves, five times, from a list that grows with the organisation's whole book.

DR1 scopes each picker to its role. Every address record carries a type — `type: 'place-of-origin'` on the Romanian farms, and so on (app/data/consignment-addresses.js:3-4) — and the picker filters the thirty-three records down to the ones whose type matches the section it was opened from, with consignor accepting consignor and exporter as aliases (app/routes.js:3457-3465). The place-of-origin picker shows nine of nine results, all of them farms, and the count line says nine out of nine rather than nine out of thirty-three, because the role list is the whole list as far as that page is concerned.

Scope each picker to the role it was opened from, so the count and the table describe the addresses that can actually be that party. This cannot be done in the frontend today: no record in the book carries a type, a category or a use, so there is nothing to filter on — the address book has to start distinguishing what a record can be used for, and the picker has to be able to ask for that. It is the same gap the contact page runs into from the other direction, and the two want one answer about what an address record is, not two. Until that lands the pickers offer choices DR1 rules out. If the answer turns out to be that a record may serve any role, DR1's filtering falls away and the finding becomes a question about the count line only.

increments.title: DR1's address picker puts the whole book on one page and narrows it as the trader types; the frontend shows five records at a time behind a Search button and pages through the rest.
increments.detail:
The picker shows five records at a time — `PAGE_SIZE = 5` (src/server/app/services/address-book/index.js:10), sliced server-side — with a govukPagination block beneath the table (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/party-picker/_address-picker.njk:64-66) and a secondary Search button that re-posts the whole form (:86-91). fe-address-picker-place-of-origin reads "Showing 5 of 13 addresses" over five rows, then "1 2 3 Next". Because the chosen record can be on a page the trader is not looking at, the picker has to restate it in an inset above the table, "Selected address: …" (:93-95) — a control that exists only to work around the paging. The page carries no client JavaScript by design (:7-11).

DR1 renders every address for the role in one table with no pagination anywhere on the page, and heads it "Select an address" with a live count, "Showing 9 out of 9 results" (app/views/consignment-address-select.html:93-97). The search control is a `type="search"` input with a magnifier button that does not submit (:70-90); typing in it hides non-matching rows and rewrites the count as the trader types. dr1-consignment-address-select shows all nine records at once, so a chosen radio is always visible next to Save and continue.

Show the whole role list on one page: drop PAGE_SIZE and the pagination block, put the count line above the table, and let search narrow the rendered list rather than fetch a new page. The frontend's stated no-JS baseline is the constraint DR1 does not have — DR1's magnifier button is `type="button"` and a no-JS Enter discards the query, so copying it verbatim would lose a working search for a trader without JavaScript. The portable half is one page, no pagination, count above the table, with the existing server-side search kept as the no-JS fallback and a filter layered on top. The "Selected address:" inset can go once the chosen row is always on screen. This assumes an organisation's book stays small enough for one page; if it will not, the finding is about the count line and the search behaviour rather than about removing pagination.

FALSIFIED BY: Pagination appearing in DR1's consignment-address-select template, or an address book large enough that one page is not viable.

increments.title: DR1 lets a trader copy an address they have already given into a second party role in one click; the frontend tells them the roles are usually the same and makes them pick again.
increments.detail:
The hub row for every party offers exactly one action, an Add or Change link to that party's picker (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/controller.js:37-46). The importer hint already tells the trader the answer: "This is usually the same as the consignee. You can select a different person if needed." (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/copy/copy.en.js:32). So the frontend states the shortcut in prose and then makes the trader open the picker, search the book again and re-select the record they have just selected. Nothing named `sameAs` exists anywhere under the addresses or contact features.

Three of DR1's six sections carry a copy shortcut, rendered as a submit button styled as a link beside the normal Add link and shown only while that section is still empty (app/views/roles-and-addresses.html:83-101). dr1-roles-and-addresses-partial shows all three at once, on a hub where place of origin and consignee are answered and the sections that depend on them are not: Consignor reads "Same as place of origin | Add a consignor", Importer reads "Same as consignee | Add an importer", and Place of destination reads "Same as consignee | Add a place of destination". The flags that switch them on are `canUseSameAsPlaceOfOrigin` on consignor and `canUseSameAsConsignee` on importer and place of destination (app/data/consignment-address-sections.js:27,54,68). Pressing one copies the source party's record id, name, address lines and country into the target section and re-renders the hub with that section answered.

Add a copy action to the hub for the three sections DR1 names, shown only while the target section is empty and the source section is answered: "Same as place of origin" on consignor, "Same as consignee" on importer and on place of destination. The hub is already a POST form (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/template.njk:13-17), and a party answer is now an address-book reference rather than a copied block, so the action writes the source party's `addressId` into the target — no address data is duplicated. This depends on the hub sections finding only for where the button sits, not for whether it works.

FALSIFIED BY: A copy-from-another-party action of any kind appearing on the frontend hub or in either picker.

increments.title: DR1's "View details" opens the address's own record page in the address book; the frontend's expands the same three lines that are already in the row.
increments.detail:
The last cell of every picker row is a `<details>` disclosure whose summary reads "View details", with a visually hidden " for <name>", and which expands in place to a list of the record's lines (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/party-picker/_address-picker.njk:26-41). Most of what it shows is already in the row — the name, the address lines and the country the Name, Address and Country columns carry — and it adds two things they do not, the telephone number and the email address (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/party-picker/view-model/address-lines.js). fe-address-picker-place-of-origin renders the disclosure triangle in every row and Astra Rosales expands to seven lines against the three in the row. There is still no record history and no way to see which other notifications use the record, and the trader never leaves the picker.

The same cell in DR1 is a link, not a disclosure: "View details" goes to the address book's record page for that address, carrying a return path back to the picker (app/views/consignment-address-select.html:152, href built at app/routes.js:3562). The trader leaves the picker, reads the whole record and comes back to the same role with their place kept.

Make "View details" a link to the address record rather than an in-page expander, so the trader reads the whole record on its page and comes back to the same role with their place kept, and drop the address lines the disclosure repeats from the row. Reproducing DR1 exactly means linking to the address book's record page in the INS front-door, because that is where the record pages live and this service reads the book and never writes it (src/server/app/services/address-book/index.js:17-19) — a cross-app link with a return path, the same dependency as adding an address from the picker, and the two should be settled together. Nothing stops a read-only record page being built here instead: the address-book service already fetches one record by id, so that route is frontend-work and needs no API change. Which of the two is right is the open question, and it is the same question the add-address finding turns on.

FALSIFIED BY: An address record page existing in trade-imports-animals-frontend, or DR1's "View details" turning out to expand in place rather than navigate.

increments.title: A user can declare only five commodities and eight species in the frontend, where DR1 offers 21 live-animal commodities under their IPAFFS names and 144 species between them.
increments.detail:
The whole catalogue is a hardcoded stub: Cow, Horse, Cat, Dog and Fish, with four species under Cow and one under each of the other four (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/services/commodities/stub.js:1-26). The file's own comment says the non-Cow entries carry one representative species each so that a batch search can select across commodity codes, which is the point — they are placeholders, not a catalogue. There is no client for reference data behind it; src/server/app/sets/live-animals/services/commodities/index.js:17-45 reads the constants directly. A user importing sheep, goats, pigs, poultry, bees or reptiles cannot say so. Two of the five entries do not match DR1 even where they overlap: the frontend calls 0102 'Cow' where DR1 calls it 'Cattle', and its 'Fish (0301)' with the single species Salmo salar is not a commodity DR1 has at all — DR1's fish commodity is 'Ornamental fish' at code 030111 with Cyprinidae, Poeciliidae and Cichlidae.

DR1 holds 21 live-animal commodities under their IPAFFS names — Cattle 0102, Horse 0101, Pig 0103, Sheep 010410, Goat 010420, Chicken 010511, Turkey 010512, Duck 010513, Goose 010514, Guinea fowl 010515, Cat 01061900, Dog 01061900, Ferret 01061900, Other live mammals 01061900, Rabbit 010614, Camel 010613, Ostrich 010633, Parrot 010632, Reptile 010620, Bees 01064100 and Ornamental fish 030111 (app/data/commodities.js). Species lists go deep where the real trade does: 11 under Cattle (app/data/commodities-0102-species.js), 3 under Horse, and 106 under Other live mammals (app/data/commodities-01061900-species.js), with the remaining 18 commodities carrying one to three each — 144 species in all. increments.title: DR1 lets the user find a commodity by typing a name, a code or a Latin name into a search box; the frontend prints every species it knows as a flat checkbox list with nothing to search.
increments.detail:
What are you importing? shows five checkbox fieldsets — Cow (0102), Horse (0101), Cat (01061900), Dog (01061900), Fish (0301) — with all eight species tickable on the page at once and no input to type into. The whole control is a loop over the catalogue: src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/commodities/search/search.njk:19-29 renders one govukCheckboxes per commodity from src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/commodities/search/view-model/commodity-groups.js:3-15. Nothing narrows the list, nothing summarises what has been picked, and the only way to review a selection is to scroll the fieldsets looking for ticks. The corpus screen id fe-commodity-search is a misnomer — there is no search on the page.

DR1 asks the same question through a search control. Under a field label 'Search for a commodity', set at heading size, sits the hint 'You can search by common name (for example, cattle), commodity code (0102), or Latin name (Bos taurus).' and a single search input with a magnifying-glass button (app/views/what-are-you-importing.html:49-86). Typing three or more characters opens a results panel below the box: matched species are listed as checkbox rows grouped under a commodity header that names the commodity and its code — 'Cattle (0102)' with 'African buffalo (Syncerus spp.)', 'Banteng (Novibos spp)' and the rest beneath it. A query matching the commodity name or the code returns every species of that commodity; otherwise it returns the species whose Latin or common name matches. Ticking a row adds it to a selected-items panel that carries a count heading, a Remove control per item and a Clear all button (:100-108), so the user always sees what is on the notification without scrolling a list. Selections survive leaving and re-entering the page because they are seeded back into the control as JSON (:110-114).

Build the search control on What are you importing? — search input with its label and hint, a results panel grouped by commodity header, and a selected-items panel with per-item Remove and Clear all — and stop rendering the catalogue as fixed fieldsets. The control is client-side over a catalogue the page already holds, so nothing blocks it, but it is worth little while the catalogue is five entries: do it alongside sourcing the real catalogue, and give species their common names first so that searching by common name returns something.

increments.title: DR1 refuses to move on until the user has entered a number of animals for every species on the consignment; the frontend accepts the field left blank and saves the blank.
increments.detail:
Number of animals is validated for shape but not for presence. The rule is integerInRange with a minimum of 1 (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/commodities/consignment-details/fields.js:21-24), and that validator allows the empty string through before the digit check ever runs (src/server/app/lib/validate/validators.js:123-131). So 'ten' is rejected and '' is accepted: Save and continue succeeds, the line is stored with an empty count, and the user reaches the rest of the journey with a consignment that says nothing about how many animals are in it. The blank is not merely tolerated, it is asserted: the feature's own test posts an empty count, expects no error re-render, and expects '' to be what the line ends up holding, treating an unanswered count as uncapped rather than zero (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/commodities/consignment-details/consignment-details.controller.test.js:150-168). What the blank does not survive is the task list — the frontend's obligation model already marks numberOfAnimalsQuantity mandatory (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/obligations/sections/commodities/lines.js:61-66) and a blank counts as unfulfilled, so the commodities task stays incomplete. The gap is therefore inside the frontend as much as against DR1: the page lets a user past a field the service's own model says they must answer, and tells them nothing until the hub.

DR1 treats the count as mandatory for every live-animal species on the page. A blank raises 'Enter the number of animals' against that species' input, and a non-numeric or non-positive value raises 'Enter a whole number greater than 0' (app/routes.js:816-848). The page re-renders with the error and nothing is saved, so a DR1 consignment cannot carry a species with no count.

Make Number of animals mandatory on Commodity details — one required rule per species line, with an error naming that line. The knock-on is the frontend's own count-drop check, which today reads a blank count as 'no cap' when deciding whether identifier records would be orphaned; once blank cannot be saved, that branch has no live case and the check compares two real numbers. Update the test that currently asserts the blank saves.

The validator: integerInRange builds a Joi string with .allow(''), and an allow value short-circuits the custom digit check, so '' passes and 'ten' does not — src/server/app/lib/validate/validators.js:123-131 is the right range and the right reading. increments.title: DR1 offers each species as its common name with the Latin name in brackets — 'African buffalo (Syncerus spp.)'; the frontend offers the bare Latin binomial, so a user who does not read Latin cannot tell the options apart.
increments.detail:
Every species option is labelled with its Latin binomial alone: under Cow (0102) the four choices read Bison bison, Bos spp., Bos taurus and Bubalus bubalis; under Horse, Equus caballus; under Cat, Felis catus; under Dog, Canis lupus familiaris; under Fish, Salmo salar. There is no common name anywhere in the option set, because the catalogue does not hold one — each species is a value and a text and the text is the Latin name (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/services/commodities/stub.js:15-26), rendered straight through as the checkbox label (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/commodities/search/view-model/commodity-groups.js:3-14).

DR1 labels a species with its common name first and the Latin name in brackets — 'African buffalo (Syncerus spp.)', 'Banteng (Novibos spp)', 'Domestic cattle (Bos taurus)', 'Water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis)' — falling back to the commodity name in front of the Latin name when a species has no common name of its own (app/assets/javascripts/commodity-search.js:11-17). 123 of DR1's 144 species entries carry a commonName next to their label — every one of the 11 under Cattle (app/data/commodities-0102-species.js:3-15), the 3 under Horse and the 106 under Other live mammals, plus Cat, Dog and Ferret. The other 21, spread over the remaining 15 commodities, have none and take the fallback, so a user searching for sheep is offered 'Sheep (Ovis aries)'. The common name is not decoration: it is what DR1's search matches on first, and the search hint tells the user so — 'You can search by common name (for example, cattle), commodity code (0102), or Latin name (Bos taurus).' The results panel is ordered by that display label rather than by the Latin name, which is why Cattle opens with African buffalo rather than Bison bison (app/utils/commodity-search-data.js:1-31).

Give every species in the catalogue a common name and render the option label as 'Common name (Latin name)', falling back to 'Commodity name (Latin name)' where a species has no common name. This is presentation plus one extra piece of data per species, so it can be done in the frontend against the current stub before the real catalogue arrives — but it has to be in place before the search control ships, because DR1's search hint promises the user can find a commodity by its common name.

increments.title: DR1's dashboard tells a user which submitted notifications still need something from them with a "Submitted action required" status; the frontend can only ever say Draft, Submitted, Amending or Deleted.
increments.detail:
The status tag on a card comes from a fixed map of four journey states: Draft (blue), Submitted (green), Amending (yellow) and Deleted (grey) (src/server/app/shared/kit.js:34-51). Once a notification is submitted it reads Submitted and stays that way, so a user scanning the list cannot tell a notification that is progressing from one that is waiting on them.

Two of the four cards on DR1's dashboard carry an orange "Submitted action required" tag beside the green "Submitted" of the others (app/views/dashboard.html:269-278, values from app/data/dashboard-notifications.js:7). DR1's status filter names a wider set again — Draft, Submitted, In progress, Approved, Action required, Rejected and Complete — so the dashboard is meant to report where a notification has got to after submission, not just that it was sent.

The dashboard needs to show a post-submission status that distinguishes a notification needing the user's attention from one that does not. The frontend cannot produce one today: the status on a row is the journey's own lifecycle state and there is no field on the record that carries a decision or an outstanding requirement back from the authorities. So the record contract needs a status the authorities can set, and the list read has to return it, before the tag can be added and the status filter built on top of it. Agree the full set of values at the same time — DR1 states seven in the filter but only demonstrates three on cards, so the list has to be settled against what the service really reports rather than copied from the prototype fixture.

FALSIFIED BY: Finding any status a frontend notification card can show, other than Draft, Submitted, Amending and Deleted.

increments.title: DR1's dashboard opens with an "At a glance" band of three counted cards — Alerts, Errors and Messages — that the frontend dashboard has nothing of.
increments.detail:
The dashboard goes straight from the entry button to the list of notifications. There is no summary band, so a user has no place to find out that anything needs their attention without reading every card in the list. The template renders the heading, the intro paragraph, the start button and then the notifications heading with nothing between them (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/template.njk:27-35).

Between the entry button and the notification list, DR1 shows a band headed "At a glance" holding three cards side by side: Alerts (yellow), Errors (red) and Messages (blue). Each card shows an icon, a count, and a link below it — "View alerts", "View errors", "View messages" (app/views/dashboard.html:40-77). In the prototype the three counts are all hardcoded to zero and every link goes nowhere: getDashboardViewModel returns alertCounts of {alerts: 0, errors: 0, messages: 0} (app/routes.js:7205-7209) and the links are href="#". So the picture shows the shape of the band but the prototype never demonstrates it carrying anything.

Build a summary band above the notification list with a card per category. The layout, headings and link labels are settled by the design and can be built from the picture. What is not settled by the design is what feeds the counts and where each link goes — the prototype answers neither, because it hardcodes zero and links to "#". Nothing in the frontend's record store expresses an alert, an error or a message: the list read asks the notifications endpoint for page, sort and reference number only (src/server/app/services/persistence/records/real/lifecycle/read.js:26-34), and the row model carries reference, status, commodity, origin, arrival, consignor, consignee and two dates (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/view-model/row/index.js:10-29). So this needs an agreed source for each of the three counts and a destination page for each link before the band can be more than three zeroes.

increments.title: The frontend lets a user delete a notification and cancel an amendment from the dashboard; DR1 has neither journey, and whether they are in scope for DR1 parity is unsettled.
increments.detail:
Every card on the dashboard offers a Delete link, and a card being amended also offers Cancel amendment (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/view-model/row/actions.js:18-67). Delete leads to a confirmation page headed "Delete this notification?" saying "This cannot be undone." with a red "Yes, delete notification" and "No, return to dashboard". Cancel amendment leads to "Cancel this amendment?" saying the changes since amending started will be discarded and the submitted version restored. Submitted cards also offer Amend, which is where the amendment being cancelled comes from.

increments.title: The frontend's dashboard lists a draft so the user can resume it; DR1's dashboard cannot show a draft at all, while its own status filter offers Draft as something to filter by.
increments.detail:
The dashboard is where a user goes back to unfinished work. A draft appears in the list with a blue Draft tag and a Resume link that takes the user back to the notification's task list (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/view-model/row/actions.js:43-52). On the captured page the only notification in the list is a draft, so the dashboard is doing nothing else at that moment.

A DR1 user never sees a draft on the dashboard. The list the root view renders (app/views/dashboard.html:253-254) is filtered before it arrives: the dashboard always uses an in-progress view of the notifications, and that view drops every record marked as a draft and every record marked as submission-complete. The DR1 fixture holds eight notifications, two of them drafts and two of them completed, and only the remaining four ever appear — which is why the page reads "Show 1-4 of 4 results". Nothing in the root design offers a way to see the other four: the root view renders no tabs and no link anywhere carries a tab, and the tab links the shared code builds all point at the design release 2.1 dashboard rather than at this one. At the same time DR1's own status filter offers Draft as one of the seven statuses a user may filter the list to (app/views/dashboard.html:153), which is a status the list it filters can never contain.

This one needs a person, because DR1 states two things that cannot both be true. Either the dashboard is deliberately a list of live consignments and drafts belong somewhere else, in which case the design owes an answer to where a user resumes unfinished work and the Draft option should come off the status filter; or the dashboard is meant to list drafts like the frontend does and the exclusion is an accident. The accident reading is the more likely one on the evidence: the filtering, the tab names and the tab links are all furniture belonging to the later design release, shared by both dashboards through one view model, and the root design uses none of it except the side effect. What settles it is a designer saying whether a draft is meant to appear on the DR1 dashboard. If it is, no frontend work follows and the note is against the prototype. If it is not, the frontend's dashboard needs a stated home for drafts before anything is removed from it, because resuming a draft is the only way back into an unfinished notification today.

increments.title: The frontend sorts the notification list by four arrival and creation orders behind an "Update sort" button; DR1 shows a sort control offering Newest first, Oldest first and Arrival date that does nothing when it is used.
increments.detail:
Above the list sits a "Sort by" select offering Arrival (newest to oldest), Arrival (oldest to newest), Date created (newest to oldest) and Date created (oldest to newest), followed by a secondary "Update sort" button. Nothing happens until the button is pressed; the chosen value then goes to the notifications endpoint as the sort parameter and the list comes back re-ordered (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/template.njk:63-82, src/server/app/services/persistence/records/real/lifecycle/read.js:26-34).

DR1 shows a "Sort by:" select offering Select one, Newest first, Oldest first and Arrival date (app/views/dashboard.html:231-251). It is inert in three separate ways: the select sits in a GET form that has no submit button, no script under app/assets/javascripts submits it on change, and getDashboardViewModel reads query.sort only to mark the chosen option as selected and to build the pagination links — it never re-orders the notifications (app/routes.js:7142, 7168-7171). Choosing an option in the prototype leaves the list in exactly the order it was in.

What is in doubt is whether DR1 specifies anything here at all. Two candidate changes hang on it: renaming the frontend's four options to DR1's three plus a "Select one" placeholder, and dropping the "Update sort" button so the select applies on its own. Neither can be justified from an inert control — a select that never sorts says nothing about which orders a user should be offered, and a form with no submit button is as consistent with unfinished scaffolding as with a design intent to auto-submit. Settle it by asking the designer two questions: is the option set on the dashboard sort control part of the signed-off design, and is the sort meant to apply without a further click? A DR1 wireframe or design note showing the sort control with its intended options and behaviour would settle both; the prototype cannot.

FALSIFIED BY: Choosing an option in DR1's Sort by select and seeing the notification list come back in a different order.

increments.title: DR1 lets a user narrow the notification list to one status from a list of seven; the frontend offers no status filter at all.
increments.detail:
The whole of the filter surface is a single "Keyword or reference" box with a Search button (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/template.njk:38-56). A user with a long list who wants to see only their drafts, or only the ones that have been submitted, has no way to ask for that.

The filter sidebar carries a collapsible "Status" section holding a single select labelled Status, offering Select one, Draft, Submitted, In progress, Approved, Action required, Rejected and Complete (app/views/dashboard.html:134-163). The control is markup only: the sidebar sits outside every form on the page — the rendered dashboard has exactly one form and it is the sort toolbar — and getDashboardViewModel reads query.status but never filters the list with it (app/routes.js:7147, 7166-7171). So DR1 states the requirement to filter by status and demonstrates the control, but a click in the prototype changes nothing.

Add a status filter to the dashboard's filter panel, offering the status values the real service actually has. Two things have to be settled before it can be built. First, the list read only accepts page, sort and reference number today (src/server/app/services/persistence/records/real/lifecycle/read.js:26-34), so filtering by status needs the notifications endpoint to accept a status parameter. Second, DR1's seven-value list is larger than the four statuses the frontend can produce — Draft, Submitted, Amending and Deleted (src/server/app/shared/kit.js:34-51) — so the option set has to be agreed against the statuses the service really holds rather than copied from the prototype's select.

increments.title: DR1 saves a document the user has filled in but not yet added when they press Save and continue, stopping them if it is incomplete; the frontend's Continue throws the part-filled row away without a word.
increments.detail:
The page has two ways forward and only one of them looks at the form. Save and add another validates the row and saves it. Continue does not read the form fields at all — the post handler falls past the add branch, checks only whether any already-saved document is still being scanned, and redirects (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/documents/controller.js:255-279). A user who types a reference, picks a date, chooses a file and then presses Continue rather than Save and add another loses all three and is not told. Nothing on the page distinguishes the two buttons' effect on the row in front of the user.

Both exits look at the row. Save and add another validates every field and re-renders with errors if any is missing — dr1-upload-documents-error is that state, listing "Enter a document reference", "Select a document type", "Enter a date of issue" and "Upload a document". Save and continue applies the same validation, but only once the user has chosen a document type, treating that as the signal that a row is in progress; if the rest of the row is incomplete the user is held on the page with the same messages (dr1-upload-documents-continue-error, showing the three remaining errors with the type already chosen), and if it is complete the row is saved on the way out (app/routes.js:10173-10192). Pressing Save and continue on a completely untouched row moves on, because uploads are optional.

Make Continue read the in-progress row rather than ignore it: if any of reference, type, date or file has been filled in, validate the whole row and hold the user on the page with the same messages Save and add another produces; if it validates, save it before moving on. DR1 uses the document type as the has-the-user-started signal, so this depends on the document-type field existing; until it does, the equivalent signal is any of the three fields being non-empty. The existing scan-settling block on Continue is a frontend extra and stays.

FALSIFIED BY: Filling in a reference, a date and a file on the frontend, pressing Continue, and finding the document in the saved list or being held on the page.

finding.correction: The silent-discard claim is confirmed, and the mechanism is exactly as written: the Continue button posts action=continue (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/documents/template.njk:92), which is neither the add branch nor a remove action, so the handler falls through to the settling check and redirects without ever touching payload.accompanyingDocumentReference, the date or the multipart file (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/documents/controller.js:255-279). Nothing client-side saves it either — the only submit listener on the form is the oversize check (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/documents/client/oversize-validation/submit.js:45-57), which returns without acting when the file is within the limit. What is overstated is the illustration and the proposed rule. DR1's soft validation is keyed on the document type alone: the branch is entered only when the posted documentType is a valid option (app/routes.js:10173-10192), so a DR1 user who fills in a reference, a date and an attachment but leaves the select on "Select one" and presses Save and continue is ALSO carried forward with the row silently dropped. Slots left as written; the finding stands, narrowed.

relatedTo.why: DR1 keys the Save and continue validation on a chosen document type, which the frontend has no field for

increments.title: DR1 lets a notification carry fifteen documents and says so before the user starts; the frontend stops at ten and only mentions a limit once the user hits it.
increments.detail:
The documents obligation caps the collection at ten entries (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/obligations/sections/documents.js:24-27) and the upload page enforces it: an eleventh Save and add another is refused with the error summary message "You can add a maximum of 10 documents" (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/documents/copy/copy.en.js:73, src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/documents/form/errors.js:52-57), anchored to the saved-documents table. Nothing on the page says a limit exists until the user meets it — the requirements list under "Your file must be:" carries only a size bullet and a file-type bullet (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/documents/template.njk:43-48).

The cap is fifteen, and DR1 states it twice. It is the third bullet of the requirements list the user reads before uploading anything, "up to a maximum of 15 files" (app/views/upload-documents.html:168), and it is enforced when the sixteenth is attempted: validation short-circuits every other check and returns one error, "You can upload a maximum of 15 files", linked to #attachment (app/routes.js:9025, :9103-9112). dr1-upload-documents-limit-error is that refusal.

Raise documents.requires.maxEntries from 10 to 15, and add the count to the requirements list the way DR1 does so the user knows the limit before uploading rather than after. The frontend's cap message is reference-numbered against the maximum, so it follows the constant; only the obligation value and the new bullet are handwritten. Whether the message keeps the frontend's "documents" or takes DR1's "files" is settled in the validation-wording finding, not here.

increments.title: DR1 asks the user to choose a document type from a list of thirteen before saving a document; the frontend never asks and guesses the type from the uploaded filename.
increments.detail:
The upload form asks for a document reference, a date of issue and a file, and nothing else (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/documents/template.njk:31-58). There is no document-type control anywhere on the page. Once the file is saved the type appears in the Document type column of the saved table, but the user never chose it: the controller derives it from the filename (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/documents/controller.js:109-112) by token-matching the filename against the document-types enum, longest match wins, falling back to OTHER when nothing matches. The module's own docstring states the rule outright — "The trader does not pick a type; the filename carries it" (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/documents/derive-document-type.js:3-18). A user who uploads scan001.pdf gets OTHER; a user who renames the same file itahc.pdf gets ITAHC. The obligation model already declares accompanyingDocumentType mandatory for every document (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/obligations/sections/documents.js:30-35), so a field the model requires has no surface at all.

Between Document reference and Date of issue the card carries a Document type select labelled "Document type" (app/views/upload-documents.html:115-130). It opens on the placeholder "Select one" and offers thirteen types in this order: Intra Trade Animal Health Certificate (ITAHC), Veterinary health certificate, Air waybill, Import permit, Letter of authority (Directive 2008/61/EC), Commercial invoice, Sea waybill, Rail waybill, Bill of lading, Catch certificate, Laboratory sampling results for aflatoxin (Reg 2019/1793), Journey log, Other (app/routes.js:9000-9018). Leaving it unchosen is a validation error, "Select a document type", linked to #document-type in the error summary (app/routes.js:9124-9130) and visible on dr1-upload-documents-error. The chosen type is echoed back in the Document type column of the saved table (app/views/upload-documents.html:203,215) — on dr1-upload-documents-populated the saved row reads "Intra Trade Animal Health Certificate (ITAHC)".

Add a Document type select to the upload form, between the reference and the date of issue, bound to the existing accompanyingDocumentType obligation, with a "Select one" placeholder and DR1's thirteen options in DR1's order, and validate it as mandatory when the row is saved. Retire deriveDocumentTypeFromFilename and its test once the field is bound. Two smaller alignments come with the field rather than separately: DR1 spells ITAHC out in full as "Intra Trade Animal Health Certificate (ITAHC)" where the frontend's label is the bare acronym "ITAHC" (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/documents/copy/copy.en.js:27), and the frontend's enum carries a fourteenth type, HEALTH_CERTIFICATE (:39), which DR1 offers only to its internal testing release and not to a design-release user.

FALSIFIED BY: Finding a document-type control the user can set on the frontend's upload page, on the page itself or on any edit route reachable from a saved row.

increments.title: DR1 gives the user a drop zone that names the chosen file back to them before the row is saved; the frontend gives them the browser's own file button and whatever text the browser puts beside it.
increments.detail:
The file control is a plain govukFileUpload with no JavaScript enhancement (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/documents/template.njk:51-58). What the user sees is the browser's native widget — on the captured screen, a "Choose File" button and the browser's own "No file chosen" text. There is no drop target: a file dragged onto the page does nothing. The chosen filename is whatever the browser chooses to show, in the browser's own wording, and it is not announced to a screen reader.

The attachment sits in a dashed drop zone (app/views/upload-documents.html:172-180). Inside it a status region, marked aria-live="polite", reads "No file chosen" until a file is picked and then reads the filename — dr1-upload-documents-file-chosen shows it reading "itahc-certificate.pdf". Below the status are a "Choose file" control and the text "or drop file", so dragging a file onto the zone is offered as an equal alternative to browsing for one. The zone takes an error style of its own when the attachment fails validation, visible as the red dashed border on dr1-upload-documents-error.

Replace the plain file input with a drop zone: a polite live region that names the chosen file, a Choose file control, drag-and-drop onto the zone, and an error state on the zone itself. govuk-frontend's file upload component already ships this behaviour behind its JavaScript-enhanced variant, so the work is enabling and styling that rather than hand-rolling a widget, and the unenhanced input stays as the no-JavaScript fallback.

FALSIFIED BY: Dropping a file onto the frontend's upload page and seeing its name appear before the row is saved.

increments.title: DR1 tells the user each document can be up to 50MB; the frontend tells the user 10 MB and rejects anything larger.
increments.detail:
The first bullet under "Your file must be:" reads "smaller than 10 MB" (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/documents/template.njk:43-48). The number is not decoration: a file over 10,000,000 bytes is refused with "The selected file must be smaller than 10 MB", and the route's own payload cap is set just above it so an oversize post is caught rather than dropped (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/documents/upload-config.js:40-49). The comment beside the constant records why it is 10 and not more — it is set to stay clear of the CDP nginx ingress cap, not chosen as a policy (:40-41).

The requirements list under Attachment opens with "files that are smaller than 50MB" (app/views/upload-documents.html:166), visible on dr1-upload-documents and repeated in every error state of the page.

Raise the per-file limit to 50MB and change the bullet to match. This cannot land in the frontend alone: the 10 MB figure exists because the platform ingress rejects a larger body before the application sees it, so the ingress limit has to be raised on the deployed environments first, then MAX_FILE_SIZE_MB and MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES, then the bullet and the oversize message. Settle the unit at the same time — DR1 writes "50MB" with no space and the frontend writes "10 MB" with one.

FALSIFIED BY: Uploading a 20MB document through the frontend and having it save.

finding.frontend: The first bullet under "Your file must be:" reads "smaller than 10 MB" (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/documents/template.njk:43-48). The number is not decoration: a file over 10,000,000 bytes is refused with "The selected file must be smaller than 10 MB", and the route's own payload cap is set just above it so an oversize post is caught rather than dropped (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/documents/upload-config.js:40-49). This cannot land in the frontend alone: the 10 MB figure exists because the platform ingress rejects a larger body before the application sees it, so the ingress limit has to be raised on the deployed environments first, then MAX_FILE_SIZE_MB and MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES, then the bullet and the oversize message. Settle the unit at the same time — DR1 writes "50MB" with no space and the frontend writes "10 MB" with one.
finding.correction: Both halves of the band's argument are in the finding and both check out. The 10 MB figure is real and decimal — MAX_FILE_SIZE_MB = 10 over BYTES_PER_MEGABYTE = 1_000_000, with MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES set 1 KB above it for multipart overhead, so an oversize post is refused rather than truncated. The ingress reasoning is the comment immediately above the constant: the 10 MB is chosen to sit about 485 KB clear of a CDP nginx ingress cap of 10 MiB, which is why the number is not a policy choice the frontend can simply raise. One qualification on the band rather than the claim: what has to land first is a platform ingress configuration change, not the API, contract or persistence change the needs-backend band is defined around, so the band is being read here as its broader sense of "cannot land in the frontend alone". Raising the promise to 50MB is roughly a fivefold increase on the current ingress ceiling, and nothing in the frontend repo establishes that CDP will allow it — that is the open question the band is carrying. Slots left as written.
